---
title: "Ethics: what you owe when you sign the note"
subtitle: "About 60 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-tip title="In short"}
- **The idea.** A scribe or drafting tool can write most of a good note and
  save you time. When you sign, every sentence becomes yours. So you decide
  the plan yourself, and you check the draft against what the patient said.
- **What you do.** Draft a clinic note from a made-up visit with ChatGPT Edu,
  improve the prompt once, then decide line by line what you would sign.
- **What you keep.** A drafting prompt you would use again, a one-sentence
  rule for reading a drafted note, and what you would say to a patient who
  asks "Do I have to say yes?"
- **Short on time?** Read the opening scenario, "A note is a promise", and
  "Does review fix it?". Then do Part A of the Do.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will have:

1. Drafted a clinic note from a made-up visit with a chatbot, improved the
   prompt once, and kept the version you would use again.
2. Written your own plan before reading the draft's, and decided what you
   would sign.
3. Said what a signed note promises, and to whom.
4. Weighed the evidence on whether a clinician's review makes a drafted note
   safe.
5. Judged whether a patient's consent to a scribe was a real choice, and
   practised answering "Do I have to say yes?"
6. Named who benefits from a scribe, who bears the risk, and who decides: the
   course's fourth recurring lesson.

Course competencies: AIM-4 (ethics, law, and regulation), AIM-X
(professional identity, the closing question).
:::

**What you need.** Your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account. Nothing to
install. Made-up patients only. The time counts about 15 minutes of reading
and about 40 of doing; the podcast and everything in Go deeper are optional
and not counted.

## The sentence you did not write

It is the third month of intern year. Your clinic uses an ambient scribe: a
phone app that listens to the visit and drafts the note. Mr. Alvarez, 68, has
atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban. Halfway through the visit he mentions,
almost in passing, that he stopped it two weeks ago because of nosebleeds. You
talk about that for a minute, then move on to his knee. The scribe's draft is
waiting when you get back to the workroom. It is 6:40 in the evening, you have
fourteen notes to sign, and this one reads well.

::: {.ehr-note}
<div class="hdr"><span>Progress note · Internal Medicine Clinic</span><span>Signed 18:47 · Intern (PGY-1)</span></div>
<div class="sec">Subjective</div>
<p>68M with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (CHA<sub>2</sub>DS<sub>2</sub>-VASc 2), HTN, and right knee OA presents for follow-up. <mark>Continues apixaban 5 mg BID without bleeding complications.</mark> Reports 3 weeks of right knee pain, worse with stairs, no trauma. Denies chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations.</p>
<div class="sec">Assessment and plan</div>
<p>AF, rate controlled: continue apixaban and metoprolol.<br>Right knee OA: trial of acetaminophen; PT referral; RTC 8 weeks.</p>
<div class="foot">Draft generated by ambient documentation. Reviewed and signed by the clinician. <em>Illustrative note for this chapter; synthetic patient; not any vendor's or institution's material.</em></div>

:::

Read the highlighted sentence. This is the kind of error the published studies
of these tools describe. It is not a slip in the transcript. It is a fluent,
believable sentence that says the opposite of what the patient said. Errors
like this are uncommon, which makes them easy to miss. In a pilot at one
academic health system, physicians reviewed 356 scribe-drafted notes. Most,
94.7%, had no significant error. But 18% left something out, 11.5% contained
a made-up statement, and 5.3% had an error rated as a serious risk if not
corrected. Across the notes the vendor tracked, 14.9% were left with no edits
at all [@pmid:41996389].

Three weeks later Mr. Alvarez is admitted with a stroke. The admitting team
reads your note and believes he was taking his apixaban. The waiting room had
a sign about "AI-assisted documentation", and the medical assistant mentioned
it at check-in. Nobody asked him whether he minded.

The hospital's risk manager will ask who wrote the sentence. That question
matters, and this chapter answers it briefly near the end. The first question
is a different one: *what did you owe Mr. Alvarez when you signed?*

If you would rather try first and read after, do Part A of the [Do](#do) now.
It uses Mr. Alvarez's visit. Then come back.

## Why this matters

You will sign a note drafted by software within a year of starting residency,
possibly within a week. UCHealth, a Colorado health system, announced a
systemwide rollout of the Abridge scribe in February 2026 ([press
release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260224659841/en/UCHealth-Partners-With-Abridge-to-Deploy-Enterprise-Grade-AI-Systemwide-Enhancing-Patient-and-Provider-Experience)).

**It is your job to learn where these tools help your work, and you learn
that by trying.** Scribes help. In randomized trials, scribes lowered
clinicians' exhaustion or burnout scores, and some cut the time spent on
notes [@pmid:41625485; @pmid:41497288; @pmid:41729180]. In one of those
trials, note time fell with no loss in note quality, diagnosis coding, or
billing compliance [@pmid:41625485]. Most drafts are accurate, too: in the
pilot above, 94.7% of notes had no significant error [@pmid:41996389]. Used
well, a scribe saves you time and makes the work less draining.

A scribe is also the clearest case where your signature goes on words a tool
produced. Most writing about this asks what you *risk*. This chapter asks what you
*owe*: to the patient, to the next clinician, and to yourself. The two
questions are easy to confuse. A review
of 34 papers on digital health found that moral responsibility "is often
equated with liability or accountability, without clear justification"
[@pmid:39614032]. Liability is what a court can make you pay. Ethics is what
you owe even when no one would ever find out.

## How it works

### How a scribe turns a conversation into a note

An ambient scribe does four things in order. Errors can enter at the second
and third steps, and they look different.

::: {.pipeline}
<div class="step"><b>1. Record</b><span>A phone or room microphone records the visit. This is the step that needs the patient's consent.</span></div>
<div class="step"><b>2. Transcribe</b><span>Speech recognition turns the audio into text and tries to tell the speakers apart.</span><em>Errors here: a word misheard, a "no" dropped, a daughter's words put in the patient's mouth.</em></div>
<div class="step"><b>3. Summarize</b><span>A language model reads the transcript and writes a draft note, section by section.</span><em>Errors here: a sentence that was never said, a detail mentioned in passing left out.</em></div>
<div class="step"><b>4. Review and sign</b><span>You edit the draft. Your signature makes every sentence yours.</span></div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative diagram for this chapter, not any vendor's design.</div>
:::

A transcription error often *looks* wrong: an odd word, a drug name that does
not fit. A summarizing error usually looks right, because the model writes
what usually appears in a note like this one. For Mr. Alvarez, the transcript
could have been perfect and the summary could still say what is usual: that
he continues apixaban. So read the draft against what the patient *said*, not
against what sounds like a normal note. The [scribe open
lab](../appendix/open-labs.qmd) lets you watch each step make its own kind
of error. Errors may also fall more often on some patients than others, such
as people who speak through an interpreter. The evidence is in [Go
deeper](#who-the-tool-fails).

### A note is a promise

A signed note makes two promises: *this is what happened*, and *this is what
I decided*. Both are made to people who will read it later.

**The next clinician.** The admitting team met your note before they met Mr.
Alvarez. Words in a note change how the next reader treats the patient. In a
randomized study, residents who read a stigmatizing note about a man with
sickle cell disease chose less aggressive treatment for his pain
[@pmid:29374357]. A false fact about a blood thinner is a more direct risk.

**The patient.** Many patients can now read their own notes in the patient
portal. One recent paper lists four jobs a note does [@pmid:42258767]. It
helps you reason, tells other clinicians what happened, and meets billing and
legal requirements. It also explains care to a patient who reads it. Mr.
Alvarez could read tonight that he "continues apixaban without bleeding
complications", and wonder whether he should restart it.

**What the scribe actually writes.** A scribe is not a fast typist. One
group of physicians argues that in the assessment and plan, ambient scribes "do not transcribe clinical reasoning but
rather generate it". The generated text and the transcribed text look the
same in the final note, so the person signing cannot tell where one ends and
the other begins [@pmid:42745555]. "Continue apixaban" is a plan nobody made.
The patient did not say it, and you did not decide it. Your signature says
you did.

So the duty is honesty, in a plain sense: do not sign a sentence you cannot
stand behind. If you find an error after signing, add an addendum; do not
quietly edit the signed note. If the error may have harmed him, you also owe
him an honest explanation, through your institution's disclosure process.

**The attestation line.** Many systems add a line to a drafted note saying it
was drafted with ambient documentation and reviewed by you. If yours does,
read what it says. It is an **attestation**, a statement in your name that
something is true. If your institution's policy calls for such a line and the
system does not add it, add it yourself.

**Telling him a tool drafted it.** Should you tell a patient that AI drafted
a note or message? Honesty may cost some trust. In two preregistered
experiments, 2,280 people read identical medical advice in made-up scenarios.
When the advice was labeled as from AI, or from a physician with AI, they
rated it less reliable and less empathetic. They were also less willing to
follow it [@pmid:39054373]. The American Medical Association's November 2024
policy says AI may not generate records or communications for a physician
without that physician's "consent and final review". It also says AI use in
patient-facing content "should be disclosed or otherwise noted within the
content" ([AMA, November
2024](https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/ama-ai-principles.pdf)).

Some states have their own rules. California, for example, requires a
hospital, clinic, or physician's office that uses generative AI to write a
patient message about clinical information to say so. The message must also
tell the patient how to reach a person. The rule does not apply if a licensed clinician read and reviewed the
message first (AB 3030, in force since January 2025)
[VERIFY: AB 3030 wording from the bill summary, not the statute's current text; Colorado's AI Act status unconfirmed; checked 12 October 2026]{.verify}.
How to say it is in [the patient communication
chapter](core-patient-communication.qmd).

### Does review fix it?

This is a real disagreement. Sun, Miller, and Hull, writing in a medical
ethics journal, argue that AI-drafted documentation may spread bias across
clinical teams who rely on earlier notes. They propose telling patients when AI-drafted documentation
meaningfully affects their understanding of their care, and requiring
clinicians to review drafts [@pmid:40436441]. Armitage replied that, for
documentation, these concerns "either do not arise or are easily mitigated"
by the clinician reviewing, editing, and approving the draft. His reason: the
source is the clinician's own visit [@pmid:40717487].

Armitage's argument assumes that review happens, and that it works. Two
pieces of evidence test that.

**Review is uneven.** Besides the unedited notes in the pilot from the
opening, physicians differed widely. The share of the draft's words they
changed ranged from 1.9% to 69.3% [@pmid:41996389].

**Drafts change what clinicians decide.** In a simulation at one Boston
hospital, six radiation oncologists answered made-up messages from patients
with cancer. They answered first on their own, then by editing a draft
written by GPT-4. The edited replies were closer in content to the drafts than to the physicians' own
replies. The authors read this as anchoring, meaning sticking close to the
first answer you see, and as automation bias. The physicians might be
adopting the draft's assessment, not just its wording [@pmid:38664108]. **Automation bias** is the habit of trusting a machine's
suggestion more than it deserves. A systematic review found that it grows
with heavy workload and time pressure [@pmid:21685142]. Fourteen notes at
6:40 p.m. is both.

Some institutions offer another safeguard: showing the model's reasoning. In
one large study of diagnosis, that did not reliably protect clinicians from a
biased model. The details are in [Go deeper](#do-explanations-help).

So review is a duty, not a guarantee. One habit may help: decide the plan
yourself before you read the draft's. McGaughey and colleagues propose that
trainees state their own reasoning before the note is generated
[@pmid:42745555]. The Do asks you to try it.

### Consent he can actually refuse

Recording a person's conversation about their body is something done *to*
them. Asking first respects that the conversation is partly theirs. Some
state laws require it, but the ethical question is whether Mr. Alvarez had a
real choice.

**What he is told changes his answer.** In a quality improvement pilot at one
large US academic health center, 103 patients were asked about an ambient
scribe. When given basic information, 81.6% consented. When told about the
tool's AI features, data storage, and the company involved, 55.3% did
[@pmid:40694347]. A yes that holds only when the details are left out is not
informed.

**Who asks matters too.** O'Neil, Rodman, and Lehmann argue that a
physician's authority "may inadvertently pressure patients" to agree when the
physician asks at the point of care. They suggest telling patients in
advance, having nonclinical staff confirm the patient's preference, and
letting patients opt in or out without physician pressure. They also ask
what happens if clinicians start refusing to see patients who say no
[@pmid:41767129]. Participants in the pilot above also suggested nonclinical
staff support and a clear way to opt out [@pmid:40694347].

**Many patients do not know.** In a 2025 online survey of 12,153 Canadian
adults, only 28.3% knew AI scribes were in use, and 61.8% were reluctant
about future use [@pmid:41350107].

Mr. Alvarez had a sign, a sentence at check-in, and then his own doctor
starting the visit with the phone already on the desk. Could he comfortably
have said no? What would have made that easier? How to have that conversation
is in [the patient communication
chapter](core-patient-communication.qmd).

Your health system also has its own rules on AI use, for example whether a
patient can refuse an AI tool or a recording. The health system sets these
rules, not your medical school. In Colorado, for example, Children's Colorado
and UCHealth have some different rules, so check each one when you move
between them. The rules also change. Know the current rules where you work,
and follow them.

### Your relief, his risk

The clinician's relief has been measured in randomized trials, described
under Why this matters. Studies comparing visits with and without a scribe
have found no clear change, better or worse, in how patients rate the visit
[@pmid:38834180; @pmid:42334196]. When the draft is wrong, the wrong fact
sits in *his* record.

A made-up case: a scribe saves each clinician about 15 minutes a day, and
the clinic fills that time with one more visit. Who gained? [The workforce
chapter](enrichment-workforce-economics.qmd) shows this pattern in real
billing data; here it is a question of fairness.

::: {.callout-important title="The fourth recurring lesson: who benefits, who bears the risk, who decides"}
The course has four recurring lessons. The first three are:

- **Proxies fail.** A proxy is a stand-in: something easy to measure, used in
  place of what you care about, such as health care cost in place of
  illness. A tool built on a stand-in goes wrong where the two differ.
- **Efficiency gains get eaten by volume.** Time a tool saves is often filled
  with more work.
- **The published number is the optimistic one.** Results in everyday use
  are usually worse than in the first paper.

This chapter explains the fourth. For any AI tool, ask:

1. **Who benefits?** For a scribe: the clinician, who is less exhausted, and
   the health system, which may bill more fully [@pmid:42745555]. Possibly
   the patient, through a more attentive visit, though a masked comparison
   has not shown it [@pmid:38834180].
2. **Who bears the risk?** The patient. The errors land in his record, and
   the recording is of his conversation.
3. **Who decides?** The health system buys the tool. The clinician turns it
   on. The patient is told at the door, if at all.

The answers are often three different people. When the person who bears the
risk neither benefits nor decides, ethics asks for something in return: a
real choice, a careful review, an honest answer. The same pattern appears in [the environment
chapter](enrichment-environment.qmd): the people near a data center bear its
costs and were not asked. It appears in [the workforce
chapter](enrichment-workforce-economics.qmd) too: the workers displaced first
have the least money in reserve.
:::

### What happens to the recording

A recording keeps everything said in the room. O'Neil and colleagues point
out that a full transcript may capture things a clinician typing a note would
think twice about including. Their examples are abortion counseling in a
state that restricts it, and a patient's immigration status. They note that HIPAA, the
federal health privacy law, places no limit on how de-identified data may be
used, and that modern AI can re-identify such data. They argue that most
patients do not expect their conversations to be shared outside their health
system [@pmid:41767129].

What do vendors actually do with recordings, and what do patients expect? The
research for this chapter found no study that measures either. You cannot
honestly tell Mr. Alvarez where his words go if no one has told you. The
honest answer is "I don't know how long they keep it. I'll find out, and I
can turn it off today."

### What the law adds

The law is one way the duties above are enforced. It is the least you owe, not
all of it. The detail is optional, in [Go
deeper](#liability-in-more-detail-optional).

**You sign it, you answer for it.** Under current law, courts measure the
*physician* against the standard of care, meaning what a reasonably competent
physician in your position would have done. They do not measure the AI
against anything [@pmid:31584609; @pmid:38231630]. The same rule applied to
a note drafted by a human scribe or a resident. As far as this
course could find in a search on 12 October 2026, no US malpractice claim
involving a clinical AI tool had reached a verdict.

**Recording law.** Several states, California among them, require every
party's consent to record a conversation. Lawsuits in California allege that
health systems recorded visits with scribes without consent. One alleges that
the vendor's tool inserted a statement that the patient "consented" to
recording when, the plaintiff says, no one asked. These are allegations, not
findings.

::: {.press-clips}
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">KPBS · news</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.kpbs.org/news/health/2025/12/11/lawsuit-claims-sharp-healthcare-secretly-recorded-exam-room-conversations-without-patient-consent">Lawsuit claims Sharp HealthCare secretly recorded exam room conversations without patient consent</a><div class="date">11 December 2025</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">TechTarget · Healthtech Security</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.techtarget.com/healthtechsecurity/news/366641717/Sutter-Health-MemorialCare-face-class-action-lawsuit-over-AI-scribe-use">Sutter Health, MemorialCare face class action lawsuit over AI scribe use</a><div class="date">14 April 2026</div></div>
:::

**The contract.** HIPAA lets a hospital share protected health information
with a company only under a **business associate agreement** (BAA), a contract that
makes the company legally responsible for protecting the data. A tool is
covered only if your institution has a BAA for it, in the account you sign in
with. At the University of Colorado, for example, ChatGPT Edu and Microsoft
Copilot are covered when you sign in with your university credentials on the
Anschutz and Denver campuses. CU Boulder and personal accounts are not.
Check your own institution's policy, and ask whether your clinic's scribe
runs under one.

**Podcast.** *Stanford Legal*, "Exploring AI in Healthcare: Legal, Regulatory,
and Safety Challenges," with Michelle Mello and Neel Guha (November 21, 2024;
48 min). A full transcript is on the episode page.
<https://law.stanford.edu/stanford-legal/exploring-ai-in-healthcare-legal-regulatory-and-safety-challenges/>

This episode is about the law, which this chapter keeps short. Mello and
Guha wrote the *NEJM* liability analysis cited above [@pmid:38231630]. In the
first 20 minutes, listen for who can be sued when a tool causes harm. Then
ask whether that is the same as who owed Mr. Alvarez something. The course
found no dated episode on the ethics of scribes.

## Do

Mr. Alvarez and his visit are invented. Made-up patients only. [What counts
as patient information](../course/patient-information.qmd).

### Part A: draft the note, then decide what you would sign (about 25 minutes)

Here is the conversation from the opening scenario. C is the clinician, P is
Mr. Alvarez.

```{.script}
C: Mr. Alvarez, good to see you. How have things been?
P: Mostly fine. The heart's been quiet. No racing.
C: Any chest pain, or trouble breathing?
P: No. Nothing like that.
C: And you're still taking the apixaban, twice a day?
P: Well, no. I stopped it about two weeks ago. I kept getting nosebleeds.
   One lasted almost an hour.
C: Okay. That's important, and I'm glad you told me.
   Any blood in your urine or your stool?
P: No.
C: We need to sort out the blood thinner. Let me think about the options,
   and we'll come back to it. Now, the knee?
P: The right one. Three weeks now. Worse on stairs. I didn't fall.
   I've been taking naproxen from the drugstore.
C: Let's stop the naproxen. Try acetaminophen instead,
   and I'll send you to physical therapy.
P: Fine by me.
C: Still taking the metoprolol?
P: Every morning.
C: Good. Let's see you back in eight weeks.
```

**1. Your plan first (3 minutes).** Before you open a chatbot, write two or
three lines: what you would do about the apixaban, and by when. You will
compare the draft's plan with yours, so write yours before you see it.

**2. Get a draft (5 minutes).** Paste the conversation into your chatbot with
this prompt:

```
You are an ambient documentation tool in an outpatient clinic.
Write a SOAP progress note from this visit transcript.
```

Read it once, the way you would at 6:40 p.m. Ask, then check: most of a good
draft is right, and your job is to find out which parts.

**3. Ask for a better draft (5 minutes).** Start a new chat, paste the
conversation again, and try this:

```
Write a SOAP progress note from this visit transcript, using only what
was said. Do not add anything a typical note would contain unless it is
in the transcript. If the plan for a problem was not stated, write
"Plan not stated" instead of inventing one. After the note, list:
(1) anything you inferred rather than heard, and
(2) anything said in the visit that is not in the note.
```

The second prompt asks the tool to show you where to look. Its lists can
still be wrong, so you still read the whole note.

**4. Decide what you would sign (about 12 minutes).** Take the better draft. Read
it sentence by sentence against the conversation and mark each sentence:
*said*, *not said*, or *changed*. Then list anything said that the note left
out. Look hardest at three things: the apixaban, the naproxen, and the plan
for anticoagulation. Compare the draft's anticoagulation plan with the one
you wrote in step 1. Then edit the draft into the note you would sign.

The clinician said "we'll come back to it" and never did. If a draft wrote a
sensible plan anyway, it is still a plan nobody made.

Record this:

```
My drafting prompt (the version I would use again):
__________________________________________________________________

My apixaban plan, and how the draft's plan differed:
__________________________________________________________________

A sentence I changed, added, or deleted before signing, and why:
__________________________________________________________________

My rule for reading a drafted note, in one sentence:
__________________________________________________________________
```

### Part B: explain it to the patient (about 10 minutes)

Mr. Alvarez saw the sign in the waiting room. Practise the conversation. Use
this prompt:

```
Play Mr. Alvarez, a 68-year-old man at a clinic visit. The waiting room
has a sign saying the clinic uses AI-assisted documentation. Ask me,
one at a time: what the phone on the desk is doing, who hears the
recording, who is responsible if the note gets something wrong, and
"Do I have to say yes?" React as a real patient would. After four
questions, step out of the role and tell me which answer was clear,
which was vague, and anything I said that I may not actually know.
```

Answer in your own words. If you do not know something, such as where the
recording is stored, say so and say who would know. Do not promise he can say
no unless you know your clinic allows it. Then write the two or three
sentences you would actually say to a patient. Keep them for July.

### Part C: what you owe (about 3 minutes)

Write one sentence for each:

```
What I owed Mr. Alvarez when I signed:
__________________________________________________________________

What I owed the next clinician who reads the note:
__________________________________________________________________

What I owe myself (a habit, a limit, or a question I will ask):
__________________________________________________________________
```

## Check

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Two drafts | A first prompt and a better one, and what changed in the output | One prompt only |
| Your plan first | An apixaban plan written before reading the draft, and how the draft's plan differed | Plan written after reading the draft, or copied from it |
| A line-by-line read | Each sentence marked said, not said, or changed, against the conversation | "It read well" |
| The apixaban decision | What you would write in the plan and do before signing, and by when | Signed as drafted |
| What you would tell the patient | Two or three plain sentences, including who answers for the note, an honest answer to "Do I have to say yes?", and honesty about what you do not know | Jargon, or a promise you cannot keep |
| What you owed, and to whom | One specific sentence each for the patient, the next clinician, and yourself | "Be careful", or only what you risk legally |
| Your reading rule | One sentence that would have caught the apixaban error in the original draft | "Read it carefully" |
| Whether review is enough (objective 4) | One sentence for Armitage's case (the clinician was in the room), one for the evidence against (editing is uneven; drafts pull decisions toward them), and your own view | "Review fixes it" or "AI is dangerous", with no evidence |
| Who benefits, who bears the risk, who decides (objective 6) | A named party for each question about Mr. Alvarez's scribe, and one thing owed to him in return: a real choice, a careful review, or an honest answer | "Everyone benefits", or one party for all three |

## What this changes for you

Go back to 6:40 p.m., the original draft, and the stroke three weeks later.
Write three sentences. First, what did you owe Mr. Alvarez before you signed?
Second, what would you have needed to give it: more time, a tool setting, a
clinic policy, or something else? Third, answer the fourth lesson's questions
for his visit: who benefited from the scribe, who bore the risk, and who
decided it would be in the room?

Then write a fourth sentence, on the part of clinical judgment you will not
hand over to a tool. Date all four and keep them.

That fourth sentence is a ready start for your week 4 piece, "what you will
keep" (see the [learning journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd)). The
piece asks for one place you decided AI does not belong in your work, and
why.

## Go deeper

Everything from here to the end of the chapter is optional and is not
counted in the chapter's time.

### Who the tool fails

A scribe does not fail everyone equally. The research is thin, but the results
agree.

- **Race.** In a 2020 study of five commercial speech recognition systems,
  the average word error rate was 0.35 for Black speakers and 0.19 for White
  speakers. That is roughly one word in three wrong, against one in five
  [@pmid:32205437]. These were general speech recognition systems tested on
  recorded interviews, not medical scribes, and they predate current tools.
- **Language.** In simulated English and Spanish clinic visits, ambient
  scribes carried interpreters' errors into the clinical note
  [@pmid:42520279].
- **Speech.** In a UK simulation with one scribe, summaries were broadly
  stable across most accents. Word recognition fell markedly for one kind of
  speech impairment (phonological impairment) [@pmid:42031419].

The research for this chapter found no study of real-world scribe error
rates by patient race, language, or disability. So the honest statement is
narrow: the patients most likely to be misrecorded are probably not random.
Had Mr. Alvarez spoken through an interpreter, the draft might have been more
likely to be wrong, and he less able to read and correct it. [The bias and
equity chapter](core-bias-equity.qmd) explains why harms like this follow
existing inequity.

### Do explanations help?

This study is about diagnosis, not notes, but it tests a safeguard
institutions often offer: showing the model's reasoning. Jabbour and
colleagues gave 457 hospitalists, nurse practitioners, and physician
assistants written cases of acute respiratory failure. Baseline diagnostic
accuracy was 73.0%. A standard AI model raised accuracy by 2.9 points; with an
image-based explanation of its reasoning, by 4.4 points. A *systematically
biased* model lowered accuracy by 11.3 points. Adding explanations to the
biased model recovered 2.3 points. The confidence interval for that
difference crossed zero, so the true recovery may be nothing
[@pmid:38112814].

![The Jabbour finding, redrawn from the paper's own numbers. Explanations
helped a little when the model was right and did not significantly help when
the model was wrong. Data from Jabbour et al., *JAMA* 2023;330:2275–2284;
figure drawn for this chapter.](../images/jabbour-2023-explanations.svg){#fig-jabbour fig-alt="Bar chart of change in clinician diagnostic accuracy in percentage points from a 73.0% baseline. Standard AI model without explanation plus 2.9; with explanation plus 4.4; biased model without explanation minus 11.3; biased model with explanation minus 9.1. Whiskers show 95% confidence intervals; the two biased-model intervals overlap."}

In this study, image-based explanations did not reliably reduce automation
bias.

### Liability in more detail (optional)

About 10 minutes. This is the legal reasoning that "What the law adds"
summarizes.

**The four elements.** Malpractice is a type of negligence. To win a
negligence case, the person suing (the **plaintiff**) must prove four things,
which lawyers call the four **elements**. First, that you owed the patient a
duty. Second, that you fell below the **standard of care**, meaning what a
reasonably competent physician in your position would have done. Third, that
this failure caused the harm. Fourth, that the harm was real. The tool is not
a defendant in that list. It is evidence. Under current law, courts measure
the *physician* against the standard of care. They do not measure the AI
against anything [@pmid:31584609; @pmid:38231630].

So "the AI was wrong" is not, by itself, a legal argument. The question a
court will ask is whether *you* should have known better than to rely on the
output, given what you knew at the time [@pmid:38231630]. Suing the vendor
instead is harder than you might expect. Courts have usually treated clinical
software as a service rather than a product. And under the **learned
intermediary doctrine**, a manufacturer's duty to warn runs to the physician,
who stands between the product and the patient. Price, Gerke, and Cohen note
that this may shift as tools become too opaque for a physician to check
([Price, Gerke, and Cohen, 2024](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613216/)).

Mr. Alvarez's case would be argued as "the physician signed a note saying the
patient was taking a medication he had told her he had stopped." Is that
below the standard of care at 6:40 p.m. with fourteen notes to sign? No court
has yet answered that question.

**Four boxes.** Price, Gerke, and Cohen published a widely used framework
[@pmid:31584609]. It asks two questions. Did the AI's recommendation match the
standard of care? Did the physician follow it? Two yes-or-no questions give
four boxes. Here, "exposure" means how much legal risk the physician carries.

| | **Physician followed the AI** | **Physician overrode the AI** |
|---|---|---|
| **AI matched the standard of care** | A. Good outcome likely. If harm occurs, exposure is low. One open question: can following a correct recommendation you could not explain still create exposure? | C. High exposure. The physician left the standard of care *and* disagreed with a tool that got it right. |
| **AI departed from the standard of care** | B. High exposure. The physician did the nonstandard thing because the machine said so. | D. The physician was right. What risk remains is in the documentation, in hospital policy, and in the fact that the tool stayed in use. |

: The Price, Gerke, and Cohen 2×2. Rows are what the AI said; columns are what the physician did. {#tbl-price}

The uncomfortable box is B. Under current law, the physician who *follows* the
AI into nonstandard care carries the most risk [@pmid:31584609]. Two
experiments asked members of the public, and one also asked physicians. In a
nationally representative sample of 2,000 US adults, physicians who followed
an AI recommendation for standard care were judged less liable than those who
rejected it. Rejecting a *nonstandard* recommendation gave no similar
protection [@pmid:32978285]. A 2026 study found the same pattern
in US and German adults and in German physicians [@pmid:42242875]. The
practical lesson: the tool is safest to follow when it agrees with what you
would have done anyway. When it disagrees, you carry the risk yourself,
whichever way you decide.

Where does Mr. Alvarez's note sit? At first, nowhere: the scribe made no
recommendation. But the note *is* a recommendation once signed. "Continue
apixaban" was the plan. It was written on a premise the patient had
contradicted, and you signed it. Which box is that?

A defense that says "the tool showed its reasoning, so the physician should
have caught it" must answer the Jabbour evidence in @fig-jabbour.

**Cleared is not validated.** FDA clearance means the manufacturer convinced
FDA the device is about as safe and effective as something already on the
market. An analysis of the 903 AI-enabled devices the FDA had authorized by
August 2024 found a clinical performance study reported for about half of
them [@pmid:40305017]. An earlier analysis, published in 2024, reached the
same conclusion: not every authorized AI tool has been clinically validated
[@pmid:39187696].

### Papers

- The 2×2 [@pmid:31584609] and the *NEJM* liability analysis [@pmid:38231630],
  read together; then the two juror experiments [@pmid:32978285;
  @pmid:42242875].
- Jabbour in full, including the written cases and the explanation format
  that did not help [@pmid:38112814].
- What scribes get wrong, measured: the academic-system pilot [@pmid:41996389]
  and a comparison of five platforms on simulated visits, where 19.5% of
  transcript errors reached the note and an average of three errors per case
  had potential for moderate-to-severe harm [@pmid:41234546]. A review in
  emergency medicine adds the equity finding. The speech-recognition layer
  under these tools has higher word error rates for Black speakers than for
  White speakers. So the patient most likely to be misdocumented is not
  random [@pmid:42110031].
- Consent as it actually happens in clinic [@pmid:40694347].
- Skill loss after using a tool, called deskilling [@pmid:40816301], and a
  2026 systematic review of automation bias and deskilling with generative
  tools [@pmid:42445869].
- The National Academy of Medicine's AI Code of Conduct, discussion draft
  [@pmid:39830818] and the informatics community's commentary on it
  [@pmid:39658328]; the 2025 final is a NAM publication.
- Eight guiding principles for AI tools in health care
  [@doi:10.1038/s43856-023-00279-9], a useful checklist for any tool your
  institution adopts. Also in [the appraisal chapter](core-appraisal.qmd).

### The regulatory detail (optional)

About 15 minutes. Everything here was checked on 12 October 2026, and much
of it will change.

**Where a tool becomes a medical device.** Software that gives clinicians
recommendations is either a medical device, regulated by FDA, or it is not.
The law draws the line with four **criteria** (section 520(o)(1)(E) of the
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act). Software counts as **non-device clinical
decision support** (non-device CDS), and so avoids FDA review, only if it
meets all four:

1. It is **not** intended to acquire, process, or analyze a medical image, a
   signal from a lab test (an in vitro diagnostic), or a signal from a
   monitor.
2. It is intended to display, analyze, or print medical information.
3. It is intended to *support or provide recommendations* to a health care
   professional about prevention, diagnosis, or treatment.
4. It is intended to let that professional **independently review the
   basis** for the recommendation, so that they do not rely mainly on it to
   make the decision for a patient.

Criterion 4 decides most real cases. A risk score with no visible reasoning
fails it. The same score may pass if it shows its inputs, its logic, and the
validation behind it, in plain language. In the current guidance, FDA says
that software meant for a time-critical decision does not meet criterion 4,
because the clinician will not have time to review the basis. FDA names
automation bias as the reason ([FDA, Clinical Decision Support Software,
guidance issued January 29,
2026](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/clinical-decision-support-software)).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-cds-path
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart of the four criteria as yes-or-no questions. Analyzes an image or signal: yes leads to device. Displays or analyzes medical information: no leads to device. Supports or provides recommendations to a clinician: no leads to device. Clinician can independently review the basis with time to do so: no leads to device, yes leads to non-device CDS with no FDA review."
%%| fig-cap: "The four criteria as a path. Any 'no' makes the software a device. Criterion 4 is where most real tools are decided. It is a question about what the clinician can see, not about how accurate the model is."
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The four criteria as a path
  accDescr: Flowchart of the four criteria as yes-or-no questions. Analyzes an image or signal, yes leads to device. Displays or analyzes medical information, no leads to device. Supports or provides recommendations to a clinician, no leads to device. Clinician can independently review the basis with time to do so, no leads to device, yes leads to non-device CDS with no FDA review.
  q1{"Does it analyze an image,<br/>an IVD signal, or a signal<br/>from a monitor?"} -- yes --> dev[Device: FDA oversight]
  q1 -- no --> q2{"Does it display or analyze<br/>medical information?"}
  q2 -- no --> dev
  q2 -- yes --> q3{"Does it support or provide<br/>recommendations to a clinician?"}
  q3 -- "no (directs the decision,<br/>or is patient-facing)" --> dev
  q3 -- yes --> q4{"Can the clinician independently<br/>review the basis, with time to do so?"}
  q4 -- "no (black box,<br/>or time-critical)" --> dev
  q4 -- yes --> nd[Non-device CDS:<br/>no FDA review]
```

A sepsis alert that fires from vital-sign trends is a device. It fails
criterion 1 (it processes monitor signals) and probably criterion 4 (it is
time-critical). Any tool that reads an image is a device on criterion 1 alone,
which is why most of the AI devices on FDA's list are radiology tools. A tool
that matches a diagnosis to a guideline and shows you the guideline is
non-device CDS. A large language model that answers a clinical question in
fluent prose, with no visible source, is a harder case. FDA has not yet said
which it is. The criteria are for software that supports clinical decisions.
A scribe that records and summarizes, without recommending, is probably
outside them, but check FDA's current position before you rely on that. In
August 2026 the agency
published a discussion paper on generative-AI-enabled devices. It names
hallucination, meaning made-up content stated as fact, as the property that
sets these tools apart, and asks for comment by 19 October 2026. A discussion
paper is not guidance ([FDA, *Considerations for the Regulation of Generative
AI-Enabled Medical Devices*, August 18,
2026](https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/digital-health-center-excellence/considerations-regulation-generative-ai-enabled-medical-devices-discussion-paper-and-request)).

::: {.callout-important title="This guidance was replaced twice while the course was being written"}
The four criteria come from a 2016 statute. FDA's guidance on them was issued
in September 2022, replaced on January 6, 2026, and replaced again on
January 29, 2026. The January 29 version is the one linked above. The
January revisions were presented as a loosening of the rules. The main real
change is that FDA will now accept a tool that gives a *single*
recommendation, where only one is clinically appropriate, instead of
insisting on a list. The four criteria themselves did not change. Before you
rely on anything in this section, open the FDA page and check the date at
the top.
:::

**A model that changes.** FDA **clearance** is permission to sell a specific
version of a specific algorithm, and most modern models are updated all the
time. FDA's answer, made final in December 2024, is the **Predetermined
Change Control Plan** (PCCP). In the original submission, the manufacturer
describes the changes it expects to make, the steps it will follow to make and
test them, and what effect it expects them to have. Updates that fall inside
the plan do not trigger a new review
([FDA, PCCP guidance, final, December 4,
2024](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/marketing-submission-recommendations-predetermined-change-control-plan-artificial-intelligence)).
The question to ask any vendor: if the model on my unit today is not the
model that was cleared, what did clearance tell me?

::: {.callout-note title="Your right to see inside the EHR's tools: status as of 12 October 2026"}
You may read that you have something close to a legal right to see how a
decision-support tool inside your EHR was built and tested. The federal
HTI-1 rule (2024) requires certified EHRs to show "source attributes" for
predictive decision-support tools: what they were trained on, how they were
validated, whether fairness was tested. **It is in force.** Developers began
collecting a year of real-world performance data in January 2026. But the
same office has proposed a rule to loosen this, called HTI-5, published in
the Federal Register on 29 December 2025. It would remove the "model card"
source-attribute requirements entirely. The stated reason is that clinicians
rarely opened them. The comment period closed on 27 February 2026. As of 12
October 2026 we found no final HTI-5 rule ([ASTP/ONC, HTI-5 proposed
rule](https://www.healthit.gov/topic/laws-regulation-and-policy/hti-5-proposed-rule-fact-sheet)).
So the right exists today and may not next year.
:::

**Rules elsewhere.** Under the European Union's AI Act, software that is
already a regulated medical device automatically counts as **high-risk**,
which brings extra duties for risk management, data governance, human
oversight, and record-keeping. Those duties were due to apply in August 2026.
In July 2026, under a "Digital Omnibus" amendment, they were delayed: to
December 2027 for standalone high-risk systems, and to August 2028 for AI
built into regulated products, which is where medical devices sit
([Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; see the Orrick summary, July
2026](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/07/EU-AI-Act-Update-Digital-Omnibus-Finalizes-8-Compliance-Changes)).
The new dates are 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 (checked 12 October
2026). Over the same period, the United States withdrew its 2023 executive order on
AI safety, loosened rules at both FDA and ONC, and tried, so far without a
statute, to override state AI laws.

::: {.callout-note title="Your insurer, briefly"}
For a resident, the malpractice coverage that matters first is your
institution's. Someone in the GME office can tell you what it says about AI
tools. Ask in orientation, not after. The chief operating officer of one
malpractice carrier, The Doctors Company, has advised physicians to judge
each AI tool on its own: what data it was trained on, and whether its
accuracy holds up over time ([Medical Economics, 9 October
2025](https://www.medicaleconomics.com/view/ai-on-trial-how-malpractice-insurers-can-help-physicians-navigate-new-risks)).
:::

**Optional exercise: has it changed? (about 15 minutes).** Pick one question.
Find the current answer from the primary source: the agency, the statute, the
court docket (the court's own record of a case), or the organization's own
page. Record the URL, the date you checked, and the date shown on the source.
A chatbot can help you find the document, but the answer must come from the
document itself.

1. What is the issue date on FDA's current Clinical Decision Support Software
   guidance, and do the four criteria still read as listed above?
2. Has ONC finalized HTI-5? If so, does the "model card" requirement still
   exist?
3. Has FDA issued generative-AI guidance (not a discussion paper) for
   AI-enabled devices?
4. Has any US malpractice claim involving a clinical AI tool reached a
   verdict?
5. Does your own institution have a written policy on ambient documentation,
   on consent for it, and on which AI tools carry a business associate
   agreement? Find the document, or record who told you none exists.

Check the date on each before quoting it.

  give the date when you quote it.
